chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hammad ibn Isa, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far and Abu Abdillah (peace be upon them both), said:

I asked both of them about a man who became ill and did not fast until another Ramadan overtook him. They said: If he was cured, then delayed (paying the fidya) before the next Ramadan overtook him, he should fast the days he missed, and give in charity for each day a mudd of food to a poor person, and he must make up the fasts. And if he did not cease to be ill until another Ramadan overtook him, he should fast the days he missed, and give in charity for the first (Ramadan) for each day a mudd to a poor person, and there is no making up of the fasts upon him.

key_terms.تَوَانَى: To delay or procrastinate without a valid excuse.
key_terms.رَمَضَانٌ آخَرُ: The subsequent Ramadan, marking the deadline for fidya.
key_terms.فِدْيَةٌ: Compensatory charity given for missing a fast due to valid excuse.
key_terms.قَضَاءُ: Making up missed obligatory acts, specifically fasting.
key_terms.مُدٌّ: A traditional unit of volume measurement for food, approximately 750g.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a sick person who misses fasting in Ramadan and remains ill until the next Ramadan?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the distinction between temporary and chronic illness regarding Ramadan obligations, establishing that prolonged incapacity exempts one from qada (making up fasts) while requiring only fidya (charity). It reflects the Shia juristic principle that the burden of fasting is lifted when the condition preventing it persists through the subsequent Ramadan, emphasizing divine mercy in cases of enduring hardship.
